title: Visual practice
intent: A body of precedents to decompose into a general principle of practice. Organized by acts of reasoning and design operations, rather than a catalog of chart types.
scope: A first research chapter based on Tufte's public essays, selected publicly posted book pages, and cited original work. This is not a complete reading of his books or an exhaustive survey of visualization. Candidate principles and implementation recipes are our synthesis; they are not established empirical laws or reconstructions of historical production software.

specimens.title: Join the evidence in one place
specimens.name: Minard's campaign map
specimens.credit: Charles Joseph Minard · 1869 · studied and reproduced by Tufte
specimens.alt: Minard's map: a wide outward band and a narrow dark return band follow the army's route, with a linked temperature plot underneath.
specimens.observation: Tufte highlights the conjunction of troop size, route, retreat, temperature, and time. The source history is also available; the drawing is a constructed account assembled from records.
specimens.structure: A journey with changing quantities, branching detachments, geographic positions, and weather observations. The shared route provides the join between evidence types.
operations: Map the route into a geographic field.
Make band width proportional to remaining quantity; distinguish direction by tone.
Align a second measurement with locations along the return and annotate dates.
specimens.reading: First see the large loss; then trace where it happens; then inspect the weather and dates. One composition supports an overview and a closer investigation.
specimens.mechanic: Proportional-width flow paths plus a linked quantitative plot. This is an encoding and composition method; the sources do not document a computational layout algorithm.
specimens.recipe: Join route segments to quantities by event or location key. Project coordinates; construct ribbons with width w = k × quantity. Align related plots on an explicit shared coordinate, while preserving time labels and branches.
specimens.use: Journeys, migration, supply flows, or attrition where quantity and location matter together. A route must be a meaningful structure in the data.
specimens.limit: A compelling shared picture does not isolate causes. Temperature alone cannot account for the losses. Ribbon geometry, joins, and source uncertainty still require inspection.
specimens.test: Can a reader connect the quantitative change to the relevant location and external evidence without mentally matching separate dashboards? Can they distinguish an observation from a causal explanation?
specimens.variation: Try a single linked composition, then separate panels with the same coordinates. Keep whichever makes the joins easiest to verify.

specimens.title: Let geometry carry the process
specimens.name: Graphical railway timetables
specimens.credit: Timetable reproduced by E. J. Marey · 1885 · Tufte credits the French engineer Ibry
specimens.alt: A Paris-to-Lyon timetable plots time horizontally and distance vertically; train paths show movement, stops, and crossings.
specimens.observation: Tufte's published page explains that distance-spaced stations let line slopes indicate travel speed, while horizontal intervals indicate stops. His later bus example combines a schedule with a detailed route photograph.
specimens.structure: Repeated entities progressing through ordered locations over time. Each trip is a sequence, and all trips occupy the same field.
operations: Choose time and physical distance as axes.
Connect each trip's arrival/departure observations in order.
Use subdued guides so many trajectories remain visible together.
specimens.reading: Read one path for an itinerary, across paths for service frequency, or at an intersection for vehicles passing each other. Patterns come from the same observations as individual journeys.
specimens.mechanic: A piecewise-linear time–distance diagram. The meaningful slope is Δdistance / Δtime; a time–stage variant does not automatically measure speed.
specimens.recipe: Group records by trip; sort by timestamp; map elapsed time to x and cumulative distance to y. Repeated y at arrival and departure encodes a stop. Link the location axis to a route view when that assists the task.
specimens.use: Transport, manufacturing journeys, execution traces, and other ordered processes. For nonphysical stages, label the axis as stage or state.
specimens.limit: Equal spacing between stations changes the slope's meaning. Dense crossing lines can hide identity; direct selection or a linked table may be necessary.
specimens.test: Can a reader find a pause, compare two journeys, and explain what a steeper path means from the actual axis definitions?
specimens.variation: Compare geographic distance, process stage, and measured progress as the vertical coordinate. They answer different questions; select one deliberately.

specimens.title: Support several coherent readings
specimens.name: A table that also shows change
specimens.credit: Edward Tufte · government receipts, 1970 and 1979 · The Visual Display of Quantitative Information
specimens.alt: Two columns of countries and government receipts as a percentage of GDP, joined by light lines that show changes and rank crossings.
specimens.observation: Tufte describes several reading paths: vertical rankings, horizontal paired comparisons, and comparison of gradients. Names and exact values remain attached to the graphic.
specimens.structure: The same identified entities observed at two or more comparable conditions. Identity links the observations; numerical position supplies magnitude.
operations: Place the two conditions in aligned columns using the same value scale.
Attach names and numbers to endpoints.
Connect identities with quiet lines; resolve label collisions without silently changing values.
specimens.reading: A reader can look up one entity, compare rank at either endpoint, or search for unusually large changes.
specimens.mechanic: Aligned value columns plus entity links and typographic collision management. Rank coordinates and value coordinates are different encodings.
specimens.recipe: Map values to a common y scale; join matching entity IDs across columns. Sort label candidates, reserve text height, and displace crowded labels with leaders. Keep true point positions intact. Choose linear or log scaling according to the comparison, not appearance.
specimens.use: Before/after comparisons, changes between periods, and comparisons between scenarios or treatments with compatible units.
specimens.limit: Two endpoints hide the path between them. Crossings can crowd the display. A rank-only variant loses the size of numerical gaps; missing uncertainty should be restored where it affects the task.
specimens.test: Can the reader recover exact endpoint values and identify the largest change? Would an intermediate reversal alter the conclusion?
specimens.variation: Add intermediate observations or link to the complete series when the path matters. Let a table and a graphic share responsibility.

specimens.title: Put history beside the number
specimens.name: Sparklines inside a financial table
specimens.credit: Edward Tufte's redesign of a New York Times mutual-fund table · Beautiful Evidence
specimens.alt: Ten mutual funds in a compact table, each with a small price history beside the fund name and exact summary values.
specimens.observation: Tufte's sparkline examples add a time history to a noun and its current value. Nearby labels and numbers supply quantitative context; aspect ratio and scaling remain consequential choices.
specimens.structure: An entity table with one or more ordered measurement series for each row.
operations: Embed a small history next to each row's exact numbers.
Align time windows across comparable entities.
Provide units, endpoints, or reference ranges nearby rather than leaving a free-floating line.
specimens.reading: Scan for shared patterns and exceptions; consult the numbers for precision. A current value becomes interpretable as part of a longer history.
specimens.mechanic: Inline time-series plotting with aligned text and numeric columns. Historical small graphics predate Tufte; his writings develop the sparkline concept and practice.
specimens.recipe: Sort observations by time; retain gaps; map them into a consistent small plotting area. Use shared scales for magnitude comparisons, or explicitly label indexing or normalization. Downsample only when needed, preserving task-relevant extrema and access to originals.
specimens.use: Entity lists, system monitoring, performance reviews, inventories, and any repeated decision currently based on a single summary number.
specimens.limit: Independently scaled rows can imply false magnitude comparisons. Tiny plots can hide missingness and short events. High density does not establish readability at a particular screen size.
specimens.test: Can a reader distinguish a recent exception from a long-standing pattern and explain whether rows share a scale?
specimens.variation: Compare raw units, change from a common baseline, and indexed histories. Use the variant that answers the stated question.

specimens.title: Give layers different visual weights
specimens.name: The signal and its supporting grid
specimens.credit: Edward Tufte · Envisioning Information, pp. 53, 55, 59 · ECG and music examples credit their original makers
specimens.alt: A published page contrasts an ECG buried in a dark grid with a lighter grid, and compares music staff treatments.
specimens.observation: The posted pages show supporting grids competing with, or receding behind, the marks. They also show typography and gentle separators organizing a dense table without a heavy lattice.
specimens.structure: Several necessary information layers coexist: observations, measurement guides, labels, and annotations.
operations: Assign each layer a role before assigning its styling.
Reduce the contrast and weight of repeated supporting structure.
Keep observations and necessary distinctions legible; check interactions between adjacent marks.
specimens.reading: The eye finds the signal first and can still use the measurement scaffolding when needed.
specimens.mechanic: Perceptual layering through contrast, line weight, spacing, typography, and restrained color. No special statistical algorithm is required.
specimens.recipe: Render guides, observations, labels, and annotations as separate semantic groups. Adjust their styles independently at the target display size. Check the result without color and with reduced contrast; retain any guide that assists lookup.
specimens.use: Dense tables, maps, traces, engineering drawings, and displays with many annotations or repeated reference structures.
specimens.limit: Over-lightening can erase necessary structure or fail for readers with low vision. This is a hierarchy problem, not a mandate to remove every grid or label.
specimens.test: At the actual viewing size, can a reader see a small event and still recover its value using the guides? What disappears in grayscale or low contrast?
specimens.variation: Hold the data fixed while changing only guide weight, label hierarchy, and spacing. Compare task completion before accepting a quieter design.

specimens.title: Keep local detail inside the larger field
specimens.name: Swiss topographic mapping
specimens.credit: Swiss mountain-map excerpt reproduced and discussed by Edward Tufte
specimens.alt: A dense Swiss mountain map combines contour lines, elevations, water, settlements, transport, terrain shading, and place names.
specimens.observation: Tufte uses Swiss maps as a demanding comparison set: fine terrain detail, numerical labels, multiple coordinated layers, and local observations held in context. His separate map discussion warns that geographic area and population are different quantities.
specimens.structure: A continuous spatial field plus point, line, area, and text features tied to the same locations.
operations: Keep a common spatial registration across layers.
Differentiate topography, water, routes, and names by visual role.
Allow local lookup and regional pattern reading in the same field.
specimens.reading: Read the terrain as a whole, then find a route or exact elevation without losing location.
specimens.mechanic: Contours, terrain depiction, symbol hierarchy, and label placement. The essay does not specify the historical production pipeline.
specimens.recipe: A modern analogue could derive isolines from a scalar grid using marching squares, then combine them with registered vectors and collision-managed labels. Choose resolution and generalization for the viewing scale. This is a proposed recipe, not a claim about how this map was produced.
specimens.use: Spatial analysis and other fields with a stable coordinate system. More broadly, it is a precedent for keeping detailed evidence within a comprehensible whole.
specimens.limit: Dense mapping relies on conventions, resolution, and reader knowledge. A geographic display is inappropriate if location is incidental. Aggregated regions cannot establish individual-level relationships.
specimens.test: Can a reader answer one local and one regional question without losing context? Does the apparent prominence reflect the variable of interest or just geographic area?
specimens.variation: Test an integrated field against separate linked layers. Retain a stable frame and explicit scale in either case.

specimens.title: Make transformations comparable
specimens.name: Merge sorting as small multiples
specimens.credit: Robert Sedgewick, Algorithms in C, 1998, p. 353 · reproduced in Tufte's sparkline discussion
specimens.alt: Five columns of different input arrays show successive merge-sorting stages; increasing ordered runs are visible down each column.
specimens.observation: Tufte reproduces Sedgewick's array states as a matrix of comparable views. Each column follows an input through successive states.
specimens.structure: A process observed at multiple steps across several initial conditions. Array index and element value remain meaningful throughout.
operations: Hold the plotting grammar and coordinates constant.
Use one matrix dimension for conditions and the other for steps.
Show enough intermediate states for the transformation to be inspected.
specimens.reading: Look down a column to follow a process; look across a row to compare how the same process handles different inputs.
specimens.mechanic: The underlying computation is merge sort; the visual method is a matrix of intermediate array states. The proposed demonstration need not replicate the original implementation.
specimens.recipe: For a bottom-up reconstruction, capture the input array and the result after each merge pass of run width 1, 2, 4, and so on. Plot index against value for every state with common bounds; lay out input families as columns.
specimens.use: Algorithm explanation, pipeline debugging, model iterations, scenario analysis, and process change where readers need to compare intermediate states.
specimens.limit: Snapshots omit events between captured steps. Excess panels can become illegible. A fixed scale is valuable only when the compared measurements are compatible.
specimens.test: Can a reader identify what changed in one step and how that change differs across conditions without replaying an animation?
specimens.variation: Pair a synchronized animation with persistent key frames. Use animation for motion and the matrix for comparisons that require visual memory.

specimens.title: Show what an alternative could look like
specimens.name: Observed sequences beside randomized sequences
specimens.credit: Edward Tufte's inference discussion · interactive implementation by Adam Schwartz
specimens.alt: Synthetic study of one outcome sequence and eight shuffled alternatives with the same total wins and losses.
specimens.observation: Tufte asks readers to compare streaks with randomized seasons. Schwartz's original demonstration preserves the Boston team's win–loss totals separately for home and road games.
specimens.structure: One observed sequence and a collection of alternatives generated under explicit constraints.
operations: Specify what the alternative model preserves and changes.
Apply the same visual treatment to observed and simulated sequences.
Place them together so an apparent pattern has a comparison set.
specimens.reading: Ask whether the alleged anomaly is visibly distinctive, rather than inventing a story for every cluster.
specimens.mechanic: Constrained randomization and repeated comparable plots. These visual checks are not automatically formal significance tests.
specimens.recipe: For the synthetic study here, Fisher–Yates shuffle 48 outcomes containing 28 wins; keep the total fixed and report the longest win run. The illustration uses one stratum and does not reproduce the Boston record or Schwartz's home/road conditioning. Real applications need an appropriate null model.
specimens.use: Exploring apparent streaks, clusters, trends, and other patterns for which a defensible alternative can be generated.
specimens.limit: An unsuitable null model creates a misleading comparison. Time dependence, seasonality, and subgroup effects may invalidate unrestricted shuffling. A visual resemblance does not establish equivalence or a p-value.
specimens.test: What evidence would make us abandon the first interpretation? Do the alternatives preserve the conditions needed for a fair comparison?
specimens.variation: Compare alternative null models side by side before choosing one. Keep model assumptions adjacent to the visual.

principles.name: Start with the act of reasoning
principles.rule: Specify what the reader must compare, trace, locate, explain, or verify before selecting a visual form.
principles.basis: Tufte's explicit account of analytical design connects design decisions to reasoning about evidence.
principles.test: Give a reader a concrete task. Can they perform it, and explain what evidence supports their answer?
principles.boundary: One composition may support several reading paths. A single headline is not a requirement to discard other useful evidence.

principles.name: Make comparisons share a frame
principles.rule: Use adjacency, common scales, stable identities, and repeated structures to reduce the mental work of comparison.
principles.basis: A synthesis across slopegraphs, timetable fields, sorting states, and randomized sequence comparisons.
principles.test: Can readers compare the relevant items without remembering another screen or translating incompatible encodings?
principles.boundary: Shared axes require comparable measurements. Independent scales must be explicit when they serve a different task.

principles.name: Combine exactness with pattern
principles.rule: Let labels, numbers, tables, and graphics contribute different kinds of precision in the same reading field.
principles.basis: Tufte's table-graphics and inline histories combine lookup with a view of change.
principles.test: Can readers recover a precise value and perceive the important pattern without changing representation?
principles.boundary: Not every quantity needs a printed label. Precision must remain legible and relevant.

principles.name: Join related evidence explicitly
principles.rule: Align different evidence types through meaningful shared coordinates, identities, or events.
principles.basis: Our reading of Minard, graphical timetables, and Tufte's discussion of map layers.
principles.test: Can readers verify how the evidence is linked? Could the alignment imply a relationship the data do not support?
principles.boundary: A shared frame invites causal questions; it does not answer them by itself.

principles.name: Preserve detail within context
principles.rule: Support both the broad pattern and a local question while keeping the reader oriented.
principles.basis: Tufte's micro/macro discussion and Swiss-map comparison set; our extension to analytical software.
principles.test: Ask one overview question and one detailed question. Can the reader answer both and retain the relationship between them?
principles.boundary: Finite display resolution requires selection, generalization, or access to a closer view. Density alone is not success.

principles.name: Layer by role and visual weight
principles.rule: Distinguish observations, guides, labels, and annotations so necessary detail can coexist without competing equally.
principles.basis: Tufte's publicly posted layering pages, especially Envisioning Information 53, 55, and 59.
principles.test: Hold the data fixed; vary visual hierarchy. Can readers find the signal and still use the supporting structure?
principles.boundary: Do not confuse quiet styling with accessible contrast or eliminate guides needed for accurate reading.

principles.name: Keep the measurement contract visible
principles.rule: Preserve units, scale, population, time, transformation, and uncertainty through every representation.
principles.basis: Our synthesis from Tufte's scale-aware examples and warnings about geographic aggregation and inferential integrity.
principles.test: Can readers say what a mark measures, which population it describes, and what has been normalized or omitted?
principles.boundary: A clean layout cannot correct incompatible denominators, biased samples, or unsupported inference.

principles.name: Design for scrutiny
principles.rule: Expose sources, transformations, responsibility, and plausible alternatives alongside the conclusion.
principles.basis: Tufte's documentation proposal and randomized sequence examples, combined with Minard's source history.
principles.test: Can another analyst reproduce the displayed values and find evidence that could contradict the interpretation?
principles.boundary: Documentation and visual controls improve inspectability; they do not certify truth or statistical validity.

practice.deliverable: A concrete question and the evidence needed to answer it. Name the competing explanations worth checking.
Entities, records, units, population, time window, missingness, provenance, and meaningful comparisons.
Choose a specimen because its data relationships or reading paths match the task. Record the limits of the analogy.
Identify transforms, ordering, coordinates, encodings, alignment, layers, labels, and the role of interaction.
Use known data and retain exact values. Record algorithms and transformations separately from presentation.

practice.step: Test the intended reading and its failure
practice.deliverable: Ask readers to perform real tasks. Check exact lookup, comparisons, units, false impressions, accessibility, narrow screens, missing data, and extremes.
Save source, data, method, rationale, observed failures, reader evidence, and a bounded rule. Promote a rule only as far as the evidence supports it.

review.scope: Local Touch Atlas source and documentation reviewed; its existing analytical test suite was run. The application was not changed. The research corpus is deliberately broader than this particular tool.
review.verified: 24 tests passed on 24 October 2026. They cover calculations, fixed references, event reconciliation, export scope, assessment bands, and peer-map layout. Passing these tests does not establish reader comprehension or production performance.
strengths: Measurement and evidence contracts are separated from the display.
Observed means and assigned peer medians retain distinct definitions.
Evidence exports preserve complete histories and enough reference data to reproduce comparisons.
The peer map preserves true coordinates and uses grouping for access rather than jittering measurements.
questions: What general record should every visual study preserve: task, data structure, transforms, encodings, reading paths, failure modes, and evidence?
Which properties belong to a general practice, and which are local policies such as fewer touches being better?
Can a reader interpret the measure, reference, scope, and largest difference? The project documentation explicitly leaves stakeholder comprehension testing outstanding.
review.interpretation: The project has a sound example of keeping measurement accountable. A broader codex can add comparative precedents and a repeatable way to evaluate design reasoning. No specific new chart is recommended for the application by this chapter.
